title: Fix a Flat Bike Tire

sources.title: Tire and Tube Removal and Installation | Park Tool
How to Patch a Tire and Tube | Park Tool

steps.title: Tube or tubeless?
steps.detail: These instructions only apply to traditional tire-body-and-inner-tube setups. Decide whether your tire has an inner tube inside or is a tubeless setup.

cites.quote: Note that these instructions only apply to traditional tire-body-and-inner-tube setups.

steps.title: Look for tubeless signs
steps.detail: Manufacturers use terms such as "tubeless ready" or "tubeless compatible" for tubeless parts. Check the tire sidewall and the rim label for this wording. A tubeless ready tire bead is generally square instead of rounded, and a tubeless ready rim has a hooked sidewall. Tubeless valves have a threaded shaft with a nut pulling the head tight against the inside of the wheel, and tubeless tires usually contain liquid sealant instead of a tube.
steps.expected: You can see tubeless wording, or an inner tube inside the tire.

cites.quote: Manufacturers use terms such as “tubeless ready” or “tubeless compatible” for components mean to be tubeless.

steps.title: Tubeless: stop here
steps.detail: Tubeless tire bodies cannot be patched with stick-on patches — use a plug tool such as the Park Tool TPT-1. This guide covers inner tube tires only. See Park Tool's tubeless articles or a bike shop.
warnings: Do not use stick-on patches on tubeless tires.

cites.quote: Tubeless tire bodies cannot be patched with stick-on patches — use a plug tool such as the Park Tool TPT-1.

steps.title: Which valve type?
steps.detail: Remove the wheel from the bike first (see Wheel Removal and Installation). Three common valve types: Schrader (about 8mm wide, spring plunger inside, like a car valve), Presta (thinner, about 6mm, small locknut at the top), Woods/Dunlop. Fully threaded valve shafts may have a locking nut next to the rim; loosen and remove it before deflating.

cites.quote: There are three common types of valve stems on bicycles: Schrader (“American” type), Presta (“French” type) and Woods (also known as “Dunlop”).

steps.title: Deflate Presta valve
steps.detail: To deflate a Presta valve, unthread the locknut at the tip of the valve stem and press. Deflate the tire completely; even a small amount of air left makes the tire harder to remove. Press downward on the wheel while depressing the valve.

cites.quote: To deflate a Presta valve, unthread the locknut at the tip of the valve stem and press

steps.title: Deflate Schrader valve
steps.detail: Use a small tool such as a hex wrench to depress the plunger inside a Schrader valve. Deflate the tire completely; press downward on the wheel while depressing the valve.

cites.quote: use a small tool such as a hex wrench to depress the plunger inside a Schrader valve

steps.title: Deflate Dunlop valve
steps.detail: On a Dunlop valve, unthread the cap a few turns, then pull outward on the tip of the valve. Deflate the tire completely; press downward on the wheel while doing so.

cites.quote: On a Dunlop valve, unthread the cap a few turns, then pull outward on the tip of the valve

steps.title: Remove tire and tube
steps.detail: Push both beads toward the rim center to loosen them. Engage one tire lever under the bead, a second lever 1-2 in (25-50mm) away, and pull both toward the spokes. Move one lever 2 in (5cm) along and repeat until the bead loosens, then slide the lever around. Starting opposite the valve, pull the tube out, lift the valve from the hole. Remove the second bead to take the tire fully off.
warnings: Do not use a screwdriver, knife, or other sharp object, which might damage tire or tube.
steps.expected: Tire and tube are completely off the rim.

cites.quote: Starting opposite the valve, pull inner tube from tire. Lift valve from valve hole and remove tube from wheel.

steps.title: Find the hole in tube
steps.detail: If possible, inflate the tube to twice its normal width. Hold it near your lips or ear to feel or hear air escaping, moving around the whole tube. If that fails, submerge it in water and watch for bubbles. Mark the hole with four pen marks, one on each side, not close to the hole. The hole type hints at the cause: single small hole = thorn/wire/nail; double slits = rim pinch; hole on inside edge = rim problem; cut at valve = misaligned tube or low pressure.
steps.expected: You see bubbles or feel/hear air at one spot.

cites.quote: Inspect for air leaks by holding tube close to the sensitive skin of lips or by holding tube near your ear to hear air escaping.

steps.title: Find cause in tire/rim
steps.detail: Inspect outside of the tread for nails, glass, thorns; squeeze cuts to look inside. Wipe the inside of the casing with a rag, then carefully feel inside with fingers. Check sidewall and bead for damage. Inspect the rim cavity: rim strip torn or off-center, sharp corners, protruding spokes. Remove any object found. A damaged casing means the tire should be replaced.
warnings: Feel inside the casing carefully; glass or wire may still be embedded.
steps.expected: No objects left in the tire; rim strip intact and centered.

cites.quote: Wipe inside of casing with a rag, and then carefully feel inside with fingers.

steps.title: Patch or new tube?
steps.detail: Simply replacing the punctured tube with a new tube is always the safest and most reliable procedure. A small hole can sometimes be repaired. Large holes, blowouts and long cuts are usually not repairable. When in doubt, replace the tube.

cites.quote: When in doubt, replace the tube.

steps.title: Patch the tube
steps.detail: Lightly sand the area around the hole (no heavy pressure). If possible clean with a rag and alcohol and let dry. Pre-glued patch: peel from backing, touch only edges, center it on the hole, press firmly and roll between thumbs and fingers. A pre-glued patch is a temporary fix; replace the tube soon. For a vulcanizing (VP-1) patch, spread a thin glue layer, let it dry, then apply and hold over a minute.
warnings: DO NOT test the patch by inflating the tube while outside of the mounted tire.
steps.expected: All patch edges look stuck to the tube.

cites.quote: Center the patch to the hole and lay the patch on the tube.

steps.title: Put tube and tire back
steps.detail: Note any direction arrows on the tire. Inflate tube just enough to hold its shape and put it in the tire, valve next to the pressure label. Put valve through rim hole pointing straight to the hub. Work one bead on by hand, tuck the tube into the rim, then the second bead. Use a tire lever only as a last resort, carefully. Check both sides for tube sticking out.
warnings: Use caution when using tire levers to avoid pinching inner tube.
A crooked valve can lead to a flat tire later.
steps.expected: Beads seated both sides, no tube visible.

cites.quote: Lower tire and valve into rim valve hole and align valve so it is pointing straight toward hub.

steps.title: Inflate and check
steps.detail: Inflate to low pressure and check the molding line above the bead on both sides; it should run evenly above the rim. If it bulges up, deflate immediately and reseat. If stuck low, soapy water can help (not grease or oil). Inflate to full pressure and check with a gauge. Refit the valve lock nut finger tight. Then reinstall the wheel.
warnings: Bulging bead line: deflate immediately and reseat tire.
Use care not to blow the tire off the rim.
steps.expected: Molding line runs consistently above the rim on both sides; tire holds full pressure.

cites.quote: Look for small molding line above bead. This line should run consistently above rim.
